nameStory: Brown mustard gets its name from the brownish-yellow seeds that have been ground into spicy mustard condiment for thousands of years. Unlike the bright yellow flowers, the seeds turn a rich brown color when mature, making this plant the source of the robust, eye-watering mustard we know from delis and hot dogs.
description: Brown mustard is an annual herb that can grow 2-4 feet tall with deeply lobed, dark green leaves and clusters of small, bright yellow flowers. Originally from Asia, this escaped garden plant now grows wild in disturbed areas across New England. The plant has a distinctive upright, branching growth habit and produces long, narrow seed pods that contain the famous spicy seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, clustered at the tips of branches - crush a flower and smell the sharp, peppery mustard scent

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green leaves with deep, irregular lobes that feel slightly rough and have a spicy bite when tasted - lower leaves are larger and more deeply cut than upper ones

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, upright seed pods about 1-2 inches long that split open to reveal small, round brown seeds with a fiery mustard taste

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant growing 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel hollow and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers

habitat: Look for brown mustard in disturbed soils like roadsides, vacant lots, farm edges, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in sunny spots with rich, moist soil but tolerates poor conditions well. Often found growing alongside other weedy mustards and common disturbed-area plants like dandelions and plantains.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic lobed leaves, which are actually edible and commonly used in Asian cuisine when tender.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flower clusters bloom from June through August, followed by the development of long, narrow seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open, releasing the brown seeds - the dried plant stems often persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: The same plant that grows wild in New England parking lots is cultivated across Asia as a major leafy green vegetable - those 'mustard greens' in the grocery store are actually the leaves of this exact same species that many people consider just a weed!
confusionNotes: Brown mustard looks very similar to field mustard, but brown mustard has more deeply lobed, darker green leaves and tends to grow taller. Memory trick: Brown mustard has 'bold' features - darker leaves, taller growth, and stronger mustard taste.
contextualKnowledge: This species goes by many names reflecting its global importance as both a crop and condiment source - Chinese mustard, Indian mustard, and vegetable mustard all refer to the same plant. What New Englanders might dismiss as a roadside weed is actually one of the world's most important leafy vegetables.
compareHints: Brown mustard differs from its close relative field mustard by having more deeply divided, darker leaves and a taller, more robust growth habit. Unlike cabbage and broccoli (which are the same species), brown mustard never forms a head or enlarged flower clusters, instead producing loose sprays of small yellow flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field mustard is smaller and weedier-looking than its cultivated cousins like cabbage and broccoli, but shares their four-petaled yellow flowers (though cabbage family crops are usually harvested before flowering).
Unlike its relatives field mustard and brown mustard, wild cabbage has distinctively thick, waxy, blue-green leaves rather than thin, bright green ones.
Compared to field mustard, rapeseed is much taller and more robust with thicker stems and larger flower clusters.
